title: Chemistry Textbooks Have Been Teaching This Wrong for Nearly a Century
summary:
For nearly 100 years, chemistry textbooks have described a fundamental concept in a way that doesn't match modern evidence. Now, an international team of researchers is calling for a major revision — and exam boards are already listening.

The concept is the inductive effect, a cornerstone of structural organic chemistry. It explains how atoms influence the distribution of electrons within molecules. Think of it as a tug-of-war over electrons: one atom pulls them closer, changing how the molecule behaves. Textbooks have long taught that this influence travels through three or four bonds, weakening progressively with distance.

But research led by Cardiff University and the University of Newcastle in Australia paints a different picture. "In our latest paper, we find that the inductive effect does not behave in this way," says Dr. Mark Elliott, lead author from Cardiff's School of Chemistry. "Instead, we show that the inductive effect in a neutral molecule does not extend beyond one bond."

That's a significant shift. Organic chemists rely on the inductive effect to explain molecular structure and reactivity — why molecules have certain properties and undergo specific reactions. If its reach has been misunderstood, other explanations built on the traditional model may also need reconsideration.

The researchers didn't base their conclusion on a single experiment. They pulled together evidence scattered across scientific literature and combined it with their own consistent data set. "While some data supporting our conclusions is already available, it is not widely known," Elliott explains. "What we have done is pull all the existing data together."

The implications reach beyond the classroom. Organic chemistry underpins medicines, advanced materials, agrochemicals, and polymers. A clearer framework for electron distribution could help scientists design better products. Already, two A-level exam boards have announced reviews of how they teach the inductive effect, directly citing the research. For students, it's a reminder that science is always refining itself — even ideas we've trusted for generations.
why_it_matters: It shows that scientific knowledge is not fixed: a rule that generations memorised for exams can be overturned when evidence is gathered and re-examined, and such corrections eventually shape textbooks, exam papers and the medicines and materials built on that chemistry.

background_read: The inductive effect grew out of work by chemists in the early twentieth century, especially Christopher Ingold, the British chemist who helped build the modern picture of how electrons shift during reactions.
For decades it has been one of the first ideas students meet in organic chemistry — the study of carbon-based molecules, which include medicines, plastics, fuels and the molecules of living things.

Science correcting itself is completely normal: plate tectonics was dismissed for decades before becoming accepted in the 1960s, and doctors once treated stomach ulcers with surgery until two Australian researchers showed that bacteria were usually the cause.
This study was led by Cardiff University, a research university in Wales, and the University of Newcastle in Australia, with Dr Mark Elliott of Cardiff's School of Chemistry as lead author.

The stakes are high because A-levels are the exams taken around age 18 in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, and exam boards control what those courses contain — so their reviews can change what millions of students are taught.

perspectives.description: If the effect really stops after one bond, chemists get a clearer framework for how electrons sit in molecules, which could improve the design of medicines, advanced materials, agrochemicals and polymers. Students also get an honest view of a science that updates itself.

The inductive effect is used throughout organic chemistry teaching, and other explanations built on the traditional model may need rethinking. Teachers and students preparing for exams may find it confusing if a long-established rule is replaced while syllabuses are still being reviewed.

This is how chemistry usually progresses: evidence accumulates, competing explanations are tested, and consensus shifts slowly. Because the conclusion comes from re-analysing existing literature rather than one decisive new experiment, other chemists will want to check and challenge it.

Two A-level exam boards have already announced reviews, so the idea could soon reach classrooms and exam papers. Further experiments and updated teaching resources will be needed to test the one-bond claim and to see how far the revision spreads beyond Britain.
